workbooktitle: Recursion with the monks of Mons Komputarius
welcome:
Welcome to the 3rd programming exercise in GdP at HU!

For this exercise on recursion we are trying something new and mixing theory and practice more than before!

Many of the exercises have automated feedback. It is meant to support you but is not binding: after submission there is still a manual correction.

We hope you like the format and learn something along the way - feel free to tell us in the survey at the end whether you liked it!
cont-1-1: The monks of Mons Komputarius: a silly computer science story
introduction: We start with a silly story that uses a well-known computer science concept ...
computarius-1-1: *A traveller is looking for a solution for his unsorted cards ... And after a long journey he reaches the temple of Mons Komputarius.*
computarius-notice-1: *The pictures in the story are screenshots from Minecraft. This workbook is not an official Minecraft product and is not associated with Mojang or Microsoft.*
computarius-1-2: (The traveller storms in. He has barely crossed the threshold when he already starts shouting.)
computarius-2-1: **Head monk:** “That does not surprise me … whoever strides so fast will inevitably walk past every solution.”
computarius-notice-2: *The head monk looks at the traveller for a long time, then he speaks*
computarius-3-4: (the head monk remains silent for a long time)
computarius-3-9: (the head monk remains silent for a long time, studying the traveller and his cards)
computarius-4-2: (the head monk again remains silent for a very long time. Then he sighs and begins to speak)
computarius-4-3: **Head monk:** “My dear stranger … how long did you travel to get here?”
computarius-4-4: **Traveller:** “With the flight and everything ... about 20 hours!”
computarius-4-6: **Head monk:** “And how long will you travel back?”
computarius-5-1: (the head monk nods thoughtfully and speaks slowly and seriously)
computarius-5-2: **Head monk:** “My dear stranger … I can show you our ways. But whether you will understand them … that I cannot promise. They are not difficult … and you seem to have the time for them ... but they require a calm and special approach, which you seem to lack …”
computarius-5-3: (the head monk looks at a young monk and nods. The young monk fetches a tray and walks over to the traveller with it.)
computarius-6-1: (the head monk turns back to the traveller and speaks firmly)
computarius-6-2: **Head monk:** “Put the cards on the tray!”
computarius-6-3: (The traveller puts his cards on the tray and the young monk carries it to the head monk.)
computarius-7-1: (the head monk looks at the cards on the tray [4 7 2 9] and takes the 9)
computarius-7-2: (the young monk walks with the tray and the remaining cards [4 7 2] to the next monk.)
computarius-7-3: (This monk looks at the cards and takes the 7.)
computarius-8-1: (the young monk walks on, the next monk takes the 4.)
computarius-8-2: (the young monk walks on and the last monk takes the 2.)
computarius-8-3: (the young monk walks with the empty tray to the traveller and gives it to him.)
computarius-9-1: (the traveller looks first at the empty tray in his hand and then at the head monk in confusion. The head monk sighs.)
computarius-9-2: **Head monk:** “My dear stranger … you seek solutions, and yet you do not see a solution even when it is right in front of you …”
computarius-9-3: (the traveller keeps looking at the head monk in confusion. The head monk now speaks rather irritated.)
computarius-9-4: **Head monk:** “Stranger … give him back the tray!”
computarius-10-1: (the young monk walks with the tray to the last monk. This monk sweeps once from left to right across the empty tray and puts his 2 on the left of the tray.)
computarius-10-2: (the young monk walks on and the next monk sweeps his finger across the tray, moving the 2 to the right. He puts his card 4 on the left of the tray.)
computarius-11-1: (and so on: the next monk sweeps and puts down his 7. The head monk sweeps and puts down his 9.)
computarius-12-1: (The young monk holds out the tray with the cards to the traveller. The traveller takes it and nods.)
computarius-12-2: **Head monk:** “My dear stranger. You now know our ways. Go out and make use of our knowledge whenever it is needed. And do not worry: it does not take a temple full of monks to accomplish the task. Discipline and calm are entirely sufficient!”
computarius-12-4: (He starts to turn around and leave, but then turns back once more)
computarius-12-5: **Traveller:** “I have discipline, and I will learn calm. I do not have a temple full of monks indeed ... but I do have a large table!”
computarius-12-7: **Head monk:** “I see you have understood! Now go forth!”
computarius-12-8: (The traveller turns around. While he is still turning, the head monk adds)
computarius-12-9: **Head monk:** “... and take things a little more calmly in future!”
computarius-13-1: (The traveller leaves the temple with calm steps.)
a1prompt: Put the events in the correct order.
a1-item0: The traveller puts his cards on the tray.
a1-item1: The head monk takes the card with the highest value and has the tray passed on.
a1-item2: Every further monk takes the largest remaining card.
a1-item3: The last monk takes the last card.
a1-item4: The traveller receives the empty tray and returns it.
a1-item5: The last monk puts his card on the tray.
a1-item6: Every monk before him pushes the cards to the right and adds his card on the left.
a1-item7: The head monk adds his card on the left and pushes the cards together.

a4-row0: A monk takes the largest card from the tray.
a4-row1: A monk has the tray with the remaining cards passed on.

a2-row0: a) How many cards is the 3rd monk offered?
a2-row1: b) Which card does the 3rd monk take?
a2-row2: c) Which cards are on the tray after the 3rd monk has put his card back (from left to right, separated by spaces)?
a2-row3: d) How many monks are needed for 5 cards?

an-question: Instead of the monks, the traveller uses a table. Which technical element do the table, or the monks as a whole, correspond to?
an-opt1: The function stack with input and return data
an-opt2: The array in which the cards to be sorted are stored

stackintro:
But what exactly happens when `sort` is called? The figure shows the resulting calls: each frame on the call stack is one call, that is, one monk, with its own local variable `largest` (the card in his hand).

- **Top, way there:** each call puts a frame on the stack until the base case (empty tray) applies.
- **Bottom, way back:** the top frame returns its result and is removed. The call below uses it to assemble its own result.
stack-caption: *Figure: Call stack while sorting the cards 7 2 9 4, the way there at the top, the way back at the bottom*
a8b-caption: The traveller sorts 5 cards on his own. How many calls of `sort` are active at the same time at most?
a8c-question: What happens if the traveller brings very, very many cards?
a8c-opt0: The method is automatically turned into a loop.
a8c-opt2: The table becomes too small: the program aborts with a `StackOverflowError`.
a8c-opt3: The cards are only partially sorted, without an error message.
a7-question: What does the head monk need to know or be able to do to perform his task correctly?
a7-opt0: How many monks stand behind him.
a7-opt1: That he gets back a sorted tray with all remaining cards.
a7-opt2: Which card the last monk takes.
a7-opt3: How to combine his own card with the returned tray.
a7-opt4: How the other monks add their cards.
a7-opt5: What to do when the tray arrives empty.
a6-question: Every monk holds a card in his hand while the others continue working. Which statements about this card are true?
a6-opt0: It is passed on to the next monk.
a6-opt1: It corresponds to the local variable `largest`.
a6-opt2: It is the return value of the call.
a6-opt3: It is kept while the further calls are running.
a6-opt4: It is a global variable that all monks access.
a6-opt5: It is not needed again until combining.
functionaloutro: The recursive function as the monks use it is **functional**. This means that all data is stored either in the function's parameters, in its output or in local variables. A monk does not need to know, for example, which cards the others are holding at the moment. In the next chapter, however, we look at a recursive function that is not functional!

sec3Ex1Title: Getting to know the Eva editor
sec3Ex1Instr1: The following exercise is meant as preparation to get to know the editor. Use the programming language of your choice (Snap, Python or Java) to reproduce the figure shown on the right!
sec3Ex1Instr2:
Defining your own functions is supported as well!

Write a method `vieleck(ecken, laenge)` (polygon) that draws a regular polygon with `ecken` corners and the side length `laenge`. Also write a method `springe(weite)` (jump) that moves the turtle **without drawing** by `weite` in its current direction.
sec3Ex2Instr1: Implement the function `zeichneTurm(n)` (draw tower) recursively (without a loop): it should draw a tower of `n` bricks of width 40.
sec3Ex2Instr2: Implement `zeichnePyramide(n)` (draw pyramid) recursively. It should draw a pyramid with the side length `n*20`. Do not change the `main` function.
sec3Ex2Instr3: Fix the errors in the given program!
sec3Ex2Instr4: All clear? Good, then you are ready for the big final exercise!
kochexplain0: The Koch curve of **recursion depth 0** is a straight line segment. In the picture it is 270 long, so the curve has width 270.
kochcaption0: *Figure: Koch curve of recursion depth 0 with width 270, one segment of length 270*
kochexplain1: For **recursion depth 1** you divide the segment of recursion depth 0 into three equal parts. The middle part is replaced by the two other sides of an equilateral triangle whose peak points upwards. This turns one segment into **four** segments. Each of these segments is a third as long as the original segment.
kochcaption1: *Figure: Koch curve of recursion depth 1 with width 270, four segments of length 90 (blue), behind them the segment of recursion depth 0 (dashed grey) with the replaced middle part (dashed red)*
kochexplain2: For **recursion depth 2** you apply the same rule to **each** of the four segments of recursion depth 1. Every further recursion depth works the same way: each segment is replaced by four segments that are each a third as long as the replaced segment. The width of the curve always stays the same.
kochcaption2: *Figure: Koch curve of recursion depth 2 with width 270 (blue), behind it the Koch curve of recursion depth 1 (dashed grey)*
k1-caption: The Koch curve is 270 wide. For each recursion depth, state how many segments it consists of and how long one of these segments is.
sec4Ex2Instr1: Program the method `koch(double laenge, int tiefe)` (length, depth), which draws a Koch curve recursively, and use it to draw the Koch snowflake. The Koch snowflake consists of a triangle of Koch curves!
sec4Ex2Instr2: With that, the hardest exercise is done. Happy holidays!
